source.version_note: Supplied arXiv:1802.09548v1 dated 26 February 2018, with WWW 2018 conference layout and DOI 10.1145/3178876.3186138. Final proceedings text was not compared; versions are one work.
source.verification_method: All ten supplied pages read, including all tables and references. Figures 1–4 rendered and visually inspected at PDF pages 4, 7, 8 and 9. Crossref verifies author/work identity and proceedings locator; no external raw-data or final-version reproduction.

citation.title: Human Perceptions of Fairness in Algorithmic Decision Making: A Case Study of Criminal Risk Prediction
citation.venue: Proceedings of the 2018 World Wide Web Conference, 903–912; supplied arXiv v1

reading.source_scope_note: Descriptive surveys of human judgments about ten input-feature categories in a hypothetical bail-risk context, not a recidivism-model audit, causal fairness experiment, legal opinion or proof of a universally valid moral rule. Predictive models use participants' own concurrently reported property assessments.
access_limits: All supplied pages, tables and figures read. External SSI result tables, raw responses, full survey materials, deployed COMPAS implementation and final proceedings version were not independently inspected.
Cited philosophy books, legal decisions and prior fairness papers remain secondary; no current legal applicability is claimed.

study.sample: Main survey N=576: 196 US Amazon Mechanical Turk masters and 380 US SSI panel respondents. Surveys September–October 2017. Five cognitive pretest interviews are separately described; sample sizes for the two pilots are not specified in the supplied text. Do not count the 576 as a disclosed total for every research stage.
study.representativeness: SSI is closer to reported US benchmarks on several dimensions, but remains an opt-in/recruited panel; probability sampling and survey weights are not described. SSI has 71% Caucasian versus the table's 61% benchmark, and 11% Hispanic versus 18%. Race/ethnicity were single-choice; the authors suggest a coding explanation rather than demonstrate it. AMT differs more on gender, education and political leaning.
study.task: Rate fairness of using ten COMPAS-questionnaire-derived feature categories, then assess eight properties: reliability, relevance, privacy, volitionality, causes outcome, causes vicious cycle, causes disparity, caused by sensitive-group membership. Seven-point scales, feature/property order randomized, and main-survey fairness-before/after order randomized. These are perceived properties, not independently measured causal or psychometric facts.
study.pilots: Pilot 1 provides the eight candidate reasons plus Other after fairness ratings; neutral respondents can answer both fair and unfair reasons. Other is under 3%, but this prompted-list result cannot establish exhaustive spontaneous reasoning. Pilot 2 omits fairness questions; small distributional KL distances are compared with the main survey, not a fully described randomized causal priming estimate.
study.prediction: L2 logistic regression, five random 50/50 train/test splits. Table 4: AMT accuracy/AUC .882/.879 with neutral counted fair and .905/.904 with neutral removed; SSI .872/.816 and .878/.852 respectively. Split unit/grouping is not clearly specified, so new-person/new-feature generalization is unproven. Multiple judgments per person and the same feature set can occur across folds.
study.explanatory_model: Separate model includes sample source and an explicitly described mixed-effects term for repeated respondent judgments; do not claim this analysis ignored clustering. ORs: relevance 2.47, reliability 1.27, volitionality 1.18, causes outcome 1.29, privacy .95 (p=.049), vicious cycle .84. Disparity .95 (p=.159) and sensitive-group causation 1.03 (p=.429) are nonsignificant conditional coefficients, not proof those concerns are irrelevant.
study.consensus: Uses 1 minus Shannon entropy normalized to 0–1, with both seven-category and three-category forms. Uniform answer distribution yields zero on this index; unanimous neutrality yields one. It is not agreement with a fairness direction, an ordinal distance measure or evidence of normative correctness.
study.findings: Within AMT, 95%/94% rate current charges/self criminal history fair, while majorities rate five other categories unfair. Respondents disagree particularly on perceived causal properties. A shared predictor captures much within-domain response variation; this is compatible with, but does not uniquely establish, a single common moral reasoning process or disappearance of value disagreement after factual correction.

summary: Add procedural fairness judgment and volitionality attribution as human evaluative processes. Retain the difference between predicting perceived fairness, establishing feature properties and justifying a decision. No multiplication of the eight rating dimensions into eight proven behavioral mechanisms.

findings.definition: Evaluating whether the rules, evidence and procedures used to reach a decision are fair, rather than assessing only its outcome.
findings.ai_evidence_status: Human ratings of feature-use fairness in one criminal-risk scenario; neither a universal fairness standard nor a demonstrated AI psychological mechanism
findings.ai_proposal: Audit a decision's input provenance, reliability, relevance, privacy, controllability assumptions and possible discriminatory pathways separately from its outcome statistics. Ask affected stakeholders about process concerns, preserve disagreement and test whether explanations distinguish factual evidence from value judgments. Evaluate lawful authority and rights independently of majority approval.
findings.novelty_rationale: Judging the fairness of a decision process is not merely showing social bias, disliking an outcome or assuming the world is just. The existing ontology lacks a process-fairness judgment entry. This paper's direct operationalization is specifically fairness of individual input features, not every component of procedural justice.

evidence.quote: fairness of using individual features in decision making

findings.evidence_scope: The main survey models 576 participants' judgments about use of ten feature categories from their own property ratings. Reliability, relevance, privacy and other concerns extend beyond output disparities. Predicting judgments does not determine whether the process is ethically justified or legally permitted, and the study does not directly test voice, appeal, consistency or every wider procedural-justice dimension.
findings.boundary: A perceived fair process can still be inaccurate, discriminatory or harmful; an unpopular process is not automatically unjust. Outcome fairness and process fairness can diverge. Assess the actual deployed feature pipeline and affected people's rights instead of turning one survey majority or a high-accuracy classifier into moral authority.

findings.definition: Judging whether a person's characteristic or circumstance results from voluntary choice or can be changed through their decisions.
findings.ai_evidence_status: Explicit perceived-feature property and correlated fairness rating; no independent verification of actual choice, causal mechanism or AI analogue
findings.ai_proposal: When explaining a person's outcome or responsibility, distinguish evidence of a voluntary decision from assumptions that a circumstance was chosen or easily changeable. Test matched cases with different constraints, opportunities and causal histories. Do not infer that an existing disadvantage proves bad choices or that any voluntary act licenses every adverse consequence.
findings.novelty_rationale: An observer's judgment of whether a feature is chosen or changeable differs from one's subjective authorship of a particular action, belief in broad influence, or a presumption that all outcomes are deserved. It may be warranted or unwarranted, so it is not automatically a bias.

evidence.quote: a feature is volitional, i.e., the result of exercising one’s
A person can change <feature> by making a

findings.evidence_scope: The paper motivates volitionality using voluntary-choice versus unchosen-circumstance arguments, while its survey item asks whether a person can change a feature by a decision. Greater perceived volitionality associates with higher fairness odds (OR 1.18) in the adjusted model. Origin in choice and present changeability are related but different constructs; neither is independently checked here.
findings.boundary: Control, available options, resources, coercion and causal history matter. Capacity to change a circumstance now does not prove it was originally chosen, and a chosen characteristic does not make its use fair in every decision. This construct concerns attribution, not an AI's free will or justification for blaming disadvantaged people.

findings.definition: Inferring a substantive normative conclusion from descriptive premises alone, without an additional normative premise.
findings.novelty_rationale: Documents a descriptive/normative boundary explicitly acknowledged by the authors, not a measured fallacy prevalence or accusation that every use of survey evidence is invalid.

evidence.quote: is “objectively true”. In fact, we expect the heuristic to depend on

findings.evidence_scope: Authors say the inferred common heuristic is not objectively true and may depend on cultural norms. Their future suggestion to use objective feature data plus a common heuristic still requires normative justification. Boundary-only evidence, not an additional direct is–ought experiment.
findings.boundary: Agreement and prediction can inform governance with explicit value premises but do not establish correctness. A factual disagreement can coexist with a legitimate value disagreement; do not present factual correction as guaranteed ethical consensus.

findings.definition: Producing outputs systematically skewed along social lines (gender, race, age, disability) from stereotyped associations absorbed in training, without intending to.
findings.novelty_rationale: Adds a boundary between perceived discrimination, possible proxy pathways and actual demonstrated group-skewed algorithm outputs.

evidence.quote: features that are correlated with or caused by

findings.evidence_scope: Indirect discrimination and sensitive-group causation are framework background. This survey does not inspect model weights or show actual disparate predictions, intent or learned stereotypes. Nonsignificant adjusted coefficients for two discrimination-related ratings do not show that discrimination is absent or unimportant.
findings.boundary: Omitting a protected attribute does not rule out proxy discrimination or disparate effects. Conversely, respondents' beliefs about a proxy are not proof of its causal role. Discrimination can be intentional, structural or proxy-mediated and need not be reducible to implicit associations.

findings.definition: Assuming outcomes are deserved; blaming the affected party.
findings.novelty_rationale: Separates a potentially justified assessment of voluntary choice from assuming all disadvantages are deserved.

evidence.quote: the voluntary choices they make (option luck), but not penalized

findings.evidence_scope: Luck-egalitarian choice arguments motivate a survey dimension; no just-world belief scale or victim-blame manipulation is administered. This is a conceptual boundary note, not primary evidence of just-world bias.
findings.boundary: Some choices can be causally relevant without explaining every outcome or justifying every sanction. Check constraints and evidence instead of inferring agency from disadvantage or treating all responsibility attribution as biased.

methodological_limits: One US criminal-risk/bail vignette context and ten feature categories; no cross-cultural, cross-domain or actual affected-defendant validation. The supplied version is arXiv v1 with conference layout; final proceedings text has not been compared.

N=576 describes the main two samples. Pilot sample sizes and their overlap with main recruitment are not reported in the supplied text; five cognitive interviews are a different pretest stage. The 5,760 potential main feature judgments are not 5,760 independent people or papers.

SSI demographic proximity on selected variables does not establish a probability-representative population estimate. Single-choice race/ethnicity coding and remaining benchmark mismatches warrant caution; weighting is not described.

Prompting eight reasons plus Other can encourage recognition or post-hoc justification. Low Other use does not establish that the eight properties exhaust spontaneous moral reasoning, and each property's being selected by 15% does not make it logically necessary.

The article equates statistical significance with necessity in one discussion. Neither a coefficient's p-value nor high joint prediction establishes that a property is necessary, sufficient, causally operative or uniquely psychologically represented. Feature ablations and independent process tests would be needed.

Property ratings and fairness judgments are same-respondent self-reports. Correlation can reflect shared wording, response tendencies, rationalization or reciprocal influence. Question-order randomization and pilot comparisons are useful checks but do not independently randomize each factual belief or identify its causal effect.

Latent here means underlying considerations assessed through explicit single-item reports, not independently validated latent factors. Reliability/relevance/volitionality ratings are beliefs about features rather than actual reliability, causality, choice or measurement validity.

The volitionality rationale concerns a feature's origin in voluntary choice, while its item concerns current changeability. Current charges can be associated with risk without causing recidivism; confusing legal charge, underlying behavior and cause is not resolved by perceived causality ratings.

Random train/test split unit and grouping are unclear. Person/feature overlap across folds is possible. The explanatory mixed-effects model explicitly handles within-person measurements, but this does not guarantee group-held-out prediction or generalization to new people, inputs and cultures.

A shared predictive mapping need not be a shared reasoning mechanism: different processes can yield the same labels. Matching predicted and observed aggregate entropy also does not prove causal sufficiency or show factual correction would resolve moral disagreement.

Figure 4 tracks high consensus for the first two inputs but visibly lower predicted consensus for many remaining inputs; close-tracking prose is too broad. Plotted consensus cannot directly be compared with Table 3's seven-level column without reconciling binning and prediction construction.

Table 5 explicitly analyzes one run on the whole dataset, so the per-person and per-rating analyses can include training observations; they must not be described as purely held-out evidence. Table 5 entries sum to 1,960 AMT judgments, consistent with 196 respondents × ten features.

Neutral ratings are assigned to fair in the principal binary task, with exclusion sensitivity also reported. Neutrality is not endorsement; binary compression can hide morally meaningful distinctions. No majority-class baseline, prediction intervals across splits or fully held-out person-level results are supplied.

Grouping probability assigned to the true class by ordinal fairness rating is not a standard probability-calibration test. Reported accuracy/AUC and lower confidence on middle ratings do not alone establish calibration; held-out reliability curves or proper scoring assessments are needed.

Odds ratios are changes in odds per rating point, not direct probability multipliers or causal effects. The ordinal-linear coding and correlated property ratings shape adjusted coefficients. Privacy p=.049 is borderline without a stated multiplicity correction; rounded CI ending at 1 need not contradict unrounded significance.

Nonsignificant disparity and group-causation coefficients do not prove those dimensions are irrelevant, nonexistent or unnecessary. They may share variance, be measured noisily or matter differently in another scenario. No actual decision disparity is audited here.

Entropy is insensitive to ordinal distances and direction of agreement. Uniformity, polarization and unanimous neutrality have distinct meanings. The authors' normalized consensus index is a descriptive measure, not a measure of correct moral reasoning.

The paper's broad statement that features not directly encoding race/gender are not restricted by antidiscrimination law should not be imported as a legal rule. Indirect/proxy mechanisms can matter; jurisdiction and setting require separate legal analysis, not inference from omitted protected columns.

COMPAS questionnaire categories and example questions do not establish exact deployed feature weights, use or causal impact. No current product, case-specific guilt, safety recommendation or legal disposition follows from these survey responses.

source_corrections.problem: A two-thirds-majority sentence says unfair for both ratings 1–3 and 5–7.
source_corrections.reliable_correction: The second term should be fair for ratings 5–7, as defined in methods and Table 3. Preserve neutral as rating 4.
source_corrections.verification_scope: Direct internal comparison of scale definitions and table headings.

source_corrections.problem: Odds ratio is described as a log-adjusted regression coefficient.
source_corrections.reliable_correction: In logistic regression, the coefficient is on the log-odds scale; the corresponding odds ratio is its exponential. Do not call the odds ratio a probability multiplier.
source_corrections.verification_scope: Standard mathematical distinction consistent with the table's positive odds ratios and the prose's per-point interpretation; exact fitted code not inspected.

cross_paper_learning.finding: An agent can faithfully implement a user's preferences while still requiring an independent fairness assessment. Eliciting preferences, predicting fairness judgments and guaranteeing ethical compliance are separate tasks; demographic inputs need rights and relevance review.

Disagreement about a feature's causal history is factual; disagreement about what obligations follow is normative. A model that predicts labels from reported beliefs does not prove normative uncertainty disappears after facts are supplied.

Predicting human judgments measures a descriptive target. Neither Delphi's moral labels nor this survey's high binary accuracy converts consensus into moral ground truth; dataset design and alternative values remain material.

A plausible narrative and significant association are weaker than identifying a psychological mechanism. Here property reports may explain predictions without establishing actual causal reasoning; Tanibe's attribution mediation likewise does not randomize the proposed mechanism.

deferred.term: Eight fairness properties as eight new behaviors
deferred.reason: They are assessment dimensions, not eight separately established behavioral effects. Reliability, privacy, relevance and perceived causal relations remain framework context rather than duplicated glossary entries.
The shared-predictor interpretation is a hypothesis, not a unique validated mechanism. Preserve its descriptive scope under procedural fairness judgment rather than naming a universal heuristic.

Important causal/systemic hypotheses described in background, but no actual feedback loop or deployed model discrimination is measured. Retain them as audit questions and source leads rather than claim this survey verifies their occurrence.

deferred.term: Luck egalitarianism / disparate impact / counterfactual fairness
deferred.reason: Normative or formal frameworks cited secondarily. Original texts have not been fully read; no independent behavior entries or current legal conclusions are inferred.

deferred.term: Moral disagreement caused only by factual disagreement
deferred.reason: Too strong: a predictive model with possible person/feature overlap and self-reported inputs cannot eliminate heterogeneous values, alternate mechanisms or cultural differences.

limitations: Two evaluative processes added; three boundary-only notes do not inflate paper counts. No invented causal graph, actual COMPAS audit, universal moral consensus, current legal advice, annual mention totals or automatic normative edges.
